title: Introduction to Java
description: Java's history, its 'write once, run anywhere' model, and the roles of the JVM, JRE, and JDK.
objectives: Understand Java's design goals and history
Understand the JVM, JRE, and JDK and how they relate

content.heading: Java's History and Design Goals
content.body: Java was released by Sun Microsystems in 1995, designed around the principle of 'write once, run anywhere' (WORA): a program compiled on one platform should run unmodified on any platform with a compatible Java runtime. It is a statically typed, class-based, object-oriented language (though it has steadily added functional-style features, like lambdas and streams, since Java 8). Java's key strengths are portability, a strong standard library, automatic memory management via garbage collection, and strong tooling/ecosystem support for large, long-lived enterprise codebases.

content.heading: JVM, JRE, JDK, and Bytecode
content.body:
These three acronyms are frequently confused: the JDK (Java Development Kit) is the full toolkit for developers — includes the compiler (javac) and everything needed to build Java programs. The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) is what's needed to run (not build) Java programs — the JVM plus the core class libraries. The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) is the actual engine that executes compiled Java programs; it's what makes 'write once, run anywhere' possible, since a JVM implementation is built separately for each platform, but all of them execute the same bytecode.

Compilation in Java happens in two conceptual stages: javac compiles .java source files into .class files containing bytecode — a platform-independent intermediate representation, not native machine code. When you run a program (java ClassName), the JVM loads that bytecode and executes it, either by interpreting it directly or by compiling hot code paths to native machine code at runtime via Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation for better performance.

content.explanation: javac performs the source-to-bytecode compilation step; java then launches the JVM to execute that bytecode. The same .class file could be copied to a different operating system's JVM and would run unmodified.

keyPoints: 'Write once, run anywhere' means compiled bytecode runs on any platform with a compatible JVM
JDK = development toolkit (includes javac); JRE = runtime environment; JVM = the execution engine itself
javac compiles .java source into platform-independent .class bytecode
The JVM interprets bytecode and JIT-compiles hot paths to native code at runtime
commonMistakes: Confusing the JDK, JRE, and JVM as if they were interchangeable terms
Assuming Java 'compiles to machine code' the same way C does — it compiles to bytecode, executed by the JVM
Trying to run java on a .java source file instead of the compiled .class file (or the class name)
